 Dunleavy's tenure
 Gov. Mike Dunleavy is in the final year of his eight-year tenure. Name what you see as his most significant policy successes and challenges, and describe how you would have handled the policy challenges differently.
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Gov. Dunleavy is in the last year of two terms. Credit where it is due.
 He took office after years of job losses. Unemployment is lower than in 2018. The Permanent Fund is larger. Oil production stopped sliding and started climbing. He pushed back on federal overreach, kept Alaska in the resource fight, and reopened the economy when others wanted it shut. The Alaska Reads Act showed common ground on education is possible. Those things happened on his watch.
 The kitchen table did not get the same attention. Housing is out of reach. Heat, fuel and groceries still punish working families, and rural Alaska pays the worst of it. The budget is still year to year. The gas line is still a speech. Young people are still leaving. Relationships with the Legislature broke down too often, and Alaska paid for the stalemate.
 I would have done a better job fostering relationships and working with the Legislature. A governor who cannot build a working majority does not deliver for families. Energy cost would be job one: in-state gas, generation and transmission that lower bills in Anchorage, Fairbanks and the Bush. 
 I backed Gov. Dunleavy. I respect the fights he won. The job now is the reality Alaskans live with, not the record we recite.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Alaska has suffered immensely through the Dunleavy Administration. I think it’s fair to describe our governor’s eight years as a failure. Alaska has lost working-age population. Our schools are closing. Our ferry system is a shell of itself. Faith in our fisheries management is at the lowest level I can remember in my adult life. Alaskans generally feel like our state is headed in the wrong direction. Dunleavy’s vetoes, which often come without explanation, represent a failure of governance.
 My governing philosophy is the opposite: start with coalitions, not confrontation. As a legislator, I chaired the House State Affairs Committee for six years, helped build cross-partisan coalitions that passed ethics reform (banning lobbyists from buying legislators food and drink) and reduced halibut and Chinook bottom trawl bycatch at the North Pacific Council. I won five elections in a district that voted for Donald Trump by focusing on the issues that voters really care about. 
 If elected governor, I will set out goals for Alaska’s future, engage collaboratively with the legislature to move toward those goals, and finally get Alaska back on track to economic growth, stable and sustainable public services, and lower costs like electricity and housing.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 Gov. Dunleavy deserves credit for defending Alaska’s economic future, standing up to federal overreach, advancing resource development and maintaining fiscal discipline through difficult years.
 But Alaskans are still hurting. Families are leaving. Energy costs are too high. Housing is too expensive. We’re losing population and struggling to compete. That’s not good enough for a state with Alaska’s resources and potential.
 We need to stop managing decline and start building growth. I want to open more land for Alaskans to own, accelerate infrastructure, reduce permitting delays, lower energy costs and make it easier for families to stay, work, raise their kids and build wealth here.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 PFD calculation
 How do you think the Permanent Fund dividend should be calculated?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 The dividend should be calculated by the statutory fixed formula, not by whatever Juneau feels like that year.
 The Permanent Fund belongs to Alaskans. Unfortunately, the way it currently sits, it needs to be restored from mismanagement and overspending in Juneau (because) it can't be delivered.
 I will not support a system where legislators shrink the check to paper over spending.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 I think the current formula needs to be rewritten as a part of a broader fiscal compromise. In addition, I will work with the legislature to constitutionally protect the Permanent Fund from overspending so that it can grow in real terms to benefit future generations of Alaskans.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 The Permanent Fund belongs to the people of Alaska. Families count on that dividend, and they deserve a system they can actually count on from year to year.
 Alaskans are sick of the PFD becoming a political weapon. That isn’t fair to anyone. I support a sustainable constitutional framework that provides meaningful, predictable dividends while protecting the fund for future generations.
 But we also need to address the bigger problem: Alaska needs an economy strong enough that we aren’t constantly choosing between dividends and essential services. More production, more jobs, more investment and more people working in Alaska means more opportunity and less pressure on the state budget.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Taxes and the PFD
 Do you support levying new taxes to afford larger annual Permanent Fund dividends? Why or why not?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 No new taxes! Life is hard enough on Alaskans today.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 I do not support creating new taxes with the express purpose of paying larger dividends, but I do think we need to diversify our state revenues and close the disconnect between the health of our economy and the revenues the state government receives to provide services that a healthy economy depends on. 
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 No.
 Alaskans are already feeling the squeeze. They’re paying more for groceries, energy, housing and healthcare. Asking working families and businesses to pay even more isn’t the answer.
 You can’t tax your way to prosperity. We need to grow. The world needs what Alaska has. We should be producing more, creating more jobs, attracting more investment and putting more Alaskans to work.
 The goal should be to make the economy bigger so the state has more revenue, not make the burden on Alaskans bigger.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 School funding allocation
 Should the state change the way it allocates funding to K-12 schools? Why or why not?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Fund education early, and show the public where the money goes.
 Districts cannot run a school on a guess. The state should set the formula and release the funding on a calendar districts can actually plan around: how much they get, and when it hits the account. Late budgets force hiring freezes, midyear cuts and chaos for teachers and parents. That is Juneau failing the classroom.
 Districts should account for every dollar in plain language. How much reached a teacher and a classroom? How much went to administration, contracts and overhead? If the state writes the check, Alaskans have a right to see the spend. Alaska pays the second most in the country and has the worse outcomes. The problem is very apparent.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 I support an amendment to Alaska’s Constitution to forward-fund education. Right now, districts learn how many teachers they can keep only after the annual budget fight is over, which is one of several reasons why we keep losing great educators to the Lower 48 while class sizes climb. With forward funding, school boards would know in advance what funding levels to expect from the state and have time to make well-reasoned and well-communicated decisions about their own budgets.
 Alaska should modernize the way it funds k12 education so the formula better reflects the real cost of educating students today. The current system relies on outdated assumptions and hasn’t kept pace with inflation, rising energy and insurance costs, or the unique challenges facing rural communities. That has left school districts making repeated cuts that hurt students and make it harder to recruit and retain great teachers.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 Alaskans are hurting because our education system isn’t working well enough for their kids. That’s not right.
 The question isn’t simply whether we spend more or less. It’s whether students are succeeding. Alaska already invests significantly in education, yet too many students are falling behind. We rank near dead last in every metric in education except for funding. The vast majority of Alaska’s students cannot read at grade level. This is unacceptable. We should be first in the nation in education.
 The good news is we know what works. We simply need to implement it. We need accountability, transparency and flexibility, along with a funding system that puts students and teachers first.
 Bernadette Wilson (R) 
 Candidate declined to answer questions.

 State services
 Are there any state services currently offered in Alaska that you think should be discontinued or reduced? Are there any state services that you would like to add or expand? Please explain.
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Broad answer: I would discontinue or reduce programs that cannot show results, duplicate federal work or exist mainly to feed Juneau. Day one, I would order a top-to-bottom review of every department: mission, headcount, contracts and outcomes. If a program cannot prove it serves Alaskans at a cost we can defend, it shrinks or ends. That includes bloated administration, overlapping boards and grants that never reach the field. I will not cut troopers, teachers in classrooms, ferries that keep communities alive or the basic infrastructure rural Alaska depends on.
 What I would expand is what keeps people here. Public safety. Career and technical education tied to real jobs, not more paperwork. Permitting that actually moves housing and resource projects forward. Energy and transmission that lower bills in Anchorage, Fairbanks and the Bush. State services should make Alaska cheaper and safer to live in, not more expensive to govern.
 The test is simple. Does this help a working family stay in Alaska? If the answer is no, it does not belong on the taxpayer’s tab.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Our administration will start a multi-year process to examine how state services are delivered to Alaskans and Alaska businesses to identify redundancies and inefficiencies. By looking at the underlying laws and architecture of government, we can find savings that aren’t realizable in the normal budget cycle.
 One area where the State of Alaska has completely failed is transportation. The ferry system has become dysfunctional, and the Dunleavy era of DOT has led to Alaska forfeiting tremendous sums of federal transportation funding which our economy and infrastructure desperately need. Turning that situation around, and getting more construction dollars on the street across Alaska, is essential.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 When an Alaskan needs help from their government, they shouldn’t have to wait months or fight through a system that doesn’t work.
 Government should be measured by whether it gets results for the people it serves, not by how many programs or employees it has.
 I want to modernize government, eliminate duplication, improve technology and make state services faster and more responsive. We have tools today that could make our government dramatically better. Alaskans shouldn’t have to accept outdated systems and slow service. Government should help enable opportunity, not create obstacles.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Revenue measures
 What new revenue measures, if any, would you support implementing to balance the state budget?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Gas line, gas line, gas line. Cutting red tape for business. Allow businesses to have a fighting chance. Drive down cost. The private sector is better at solving problems for us all. Get government out of the way. Grow competition. Basic economics.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 I would work with the legislature to find reasonable new sources of revenue, including closing the S-corp loophole in our corporate income tax structure, and joining the Multistate Tax Compact to collect our share of corporate income tax from highly digitized businesses like Amazon and Microsoft. The latter measure passed the legislature with bipartisan support, only to be vetoed by Gov. Dunleavy.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 Alaskans are already paying enough. No new taxes!
 Before government asks families and businesses for more money, it needs to use the money it already has effectively. That means growing the economy, developing our resources, attracting investment and reversing population loss.
 We shouldn’t make it more expensive to live, work or build a business in Alaska. We should make Alaska the place people want to come to.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Environmental change
 Some Alaska communities are increasingly susceptible to destructive storms and environmental changes. What steps do you think the state should take to support these communities?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Alaska has always lived with hard weather. The question is whether Juneau shows up for the communities that take the hit.
 The state should stand with coastal and river towns the same way it stands with any Alaskan in a disaster: quickly, without the runaround, and with respect for people who know their own ground. That means working with local leaders, not talking over them. It means using state tools to backstop what federal agencies are slow to deliver.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Alaskans across the state, and particularly in the communities hit by Typhoons Merbok and Halong, have watched the ground literally give way beneath them. The state's job is to be a reliable partner instead of an absentee one. That means coordinating emergency response so communities aren't navigating a dozen federal agencies on their own. It means making sure Alaska receives our fair share of funding for resilience and adaptation. And it means planning protection — and, where necessary, relocation — with the people who live there. That also means partnering with critical groups across our state, like Association of Village Council Presidents and others, who understand the needs of local communities best. Finally, we have to make sure critical infrastructure — water systems, tank farms, airstrips — is up to spec so it can withstand the next record-breaking storm.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 When a storm destroys someone’s home, damages a community or threatens critical infrastructure, this isn’t an abstract policy debate. These are Alaska families watching their communities change in front of them.
 The state needs to be there with practical solutions, helping communities assess risks, coordinate resources and protect lives and critical infrastructure.
 Every community is different. Alaska needs solutions that respect local priorities and put people first rather than trying to force every community into the same model.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Outmigration
 Alaska has experienced years of net outmigration. What is the most impactful step you, as governor, would take to reverse this trend?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 People leave Alaska when the math no longer works. Fix the math.
 As governor, I would treat three things as one job: education that leads to work, a cost of living a paycheck can cover, and private-sector jobs that pay enough to stay.
 Schools have to produce more than a diploma. I would push real career and technical education, apprenticeships and trades so a kid in Wasilla or Bethel can get a skill that pays in Alaska, not a ticket to Idaho. Parents deserve schools that work. Employers deserve graduates they can hire.
 Cost of living is why families walk.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 This issue is personal to me. I’m 37 years old. I’ve seen friends across the state struggle with whether to stay in Alaska or leave. Our state’s future depends on us being able to make the case to young folks that this is not just somewhere to work for a season or two. It’s a place to put down roots, buy a home, and start a family. 
 The best thing we can do to invest in our state’s future and stop the tide of neighbors leaving for the Lower 48 is to invest in our schools, from pre-K all the way up to the University of Alaska system, and including technical and vocational schools. Good schools build strong communities, train the next generation of gifted Alaskans, and support parents in their own careers. 
 That’s priority number one. (Priority number two: lower the cost of housing and build more homes.)
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 Make Alaska affordable again.
 Every time a family leaves Alaska, we lose more than a number on a population chart. We lose a neighbor, a worker, a business owner, a teacher and a future Alaskan.
 People leave when they can’t afford to live here or can’t see a path to opportunity. That has to change.
 We need affordable energy, more housing, better infrastructure, a stronger workforce and more opportunities to build wealth. I want to put more land into the hands of Alaskans through a modern Alaska Homestead Act and be a place where businesses want to come through permitting and regulatory reform.
 Let’s make Alaska the most competitive place in North America to build, invest, hire and raise a family.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Healthcare affordability
 Alaska has some of the highest healthcare costs in the country. What do you think the state should do to make healthcare more affordable?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Alaska has some of the highest healthcare costs in the country because too few players control the market. That is not a mystery. It is simple economics.
 As governor, I would cut the red tape that keeps insurance providers from entering Alaska. More carriers in the market means more competition. More competition means pressure on premiums, networks and prices. Families and employers should not be stuck with two choices and a bill they cannot pay.
 Let more providers compete. Drive the cost down. That is how you make care more affordable in Alaska.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Alaska pays some of the highest health care prices in the country — our insurance can cost more than double what the same coverage runs in the Lower 48 — and that's a big reason families and businesses leave. There's a lot we can do without waiting.
 Protect Medicaid, which insures roughly one in three Alaskans. Expand telehealth, including for mental and reproductive health, so our rural communities don’t need an overnight trip for a routine appointment. Bring real transparency to what procedures and drugs actually cost, and use the state's purchasing power to negotiate better prices. Get rid of middlemen, like pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), that drive up costs.
 We also face a very serious shortage of doctors and nurses, which exacerbates the high healthcare costs Alaskans face. We can’t fix that overnight, but we should be making investments in training and retaining healthcare workers, which will lower healthcare costs and create well-paid jobs for young people. Right now, for example, there are far more Alaskans who are interested in nursing school than there are nursing student spots at Alaska universities. Meanwhile, we face a huge shortage of nurses in our hospitals and clinics and have to pay a steep premium to bring travel nurses to rural communities. We need to expand our pipelines for healthcare jobs.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 For too many Alaskans, getting sick can mean getting buried in medical bills. And in rural Alaska, simply getting access to care can mean traveling hundreds of miles.
 We have to address both the cost of healthcare and the way we deliver it. Through the Rural Healthcare Transformation Program, Alaska has the opportunity to make healthcare work for Alaskans again.
 That means expanding the healthcare workforce, encouraging telemedicine, reducing unnecessary regulations, fighting fraud and waste, improving accountability and demanding that the federal government fulfill its obligations to Alaska. 
 Alaskans shouldn’t have to pay some of the highest healthcare costs in the country and still struggle to get the care they need.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Energy costs
 What do you think the state should do to bring down the cost of energy for Alaska consumers?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Energy is too expensive in Alaska because we keep saying no to the projects that would make it cheaper.
 The state should say yes to responsible oil, gas, hydro, nuclear, coal generation and transmission that serve Alaskans first. In-state gas, more power on the Railbelt and real infrastructure to the Bush will do more for a family’s bill than another study. Stop burying projects in process. Set a clock on permits. If a project provides heat, power and jobs for our state, the default answer from Juneau should be go.
 Rural Alaska pays the highest price for delay. A gallon of fuel and a kilowatt should not decide whether a village can stay. Develop what we have. Build what we need. 
 Stop saying no to projects that provide for our state. That is how you bring the cost of energy down.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Lowering energy costs is one of simplest ways to make life in Alaska more affordable.
 I support an “all of the above” energy policy: Alaska needs more energy, from every source available. I support AK LNG if the economics prove the project to be viable. I support targeted royalty reduction in Cook Inlet to incent additional natural gas production. And I support fast-tracked permitting and capital investment in renewable power generation where it makes sense and will produce the cheapest power available.
 I want an efficient, fully-staffed Regulatory Commission of Alaska to keep utility operations running smoothly. I support a new General Obligation bond package for new electricity generation, transmission and storage.
 On the Railbelt, I'd aggressively push the four utilities to cooperate — shared transmission, economic dispatch, a unified grid. In rural Alaska, I’d protect the Power Cost Equalization program and invest in the local wind, solar, and microhydro projects already cutting diesel dependence. 
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 When energy costs go up, everything goes up. Families pay more to heat their homes. Businesses pay more to operate. Groceries, transportation and basic necessities become more expensive.
 Alaskans shouldn’t have to choose between heating their home and paying another bill. 
 We need an all-of-the-above energy strategy: more Southcentral gas production, the gas pipeline, major hydroelectric opportunities, new baseload generation, stronger transmission infrastructure and innovation across every form of energy.
 Alaska has enough energy to power a continent, it shouldn’t struggle to power the Railbelt.
 Bernadette Wilson (R) 
 Candidate declined to answer questions.

 Fisheries management
 Do you think Alaska should change the way it manages its fisheries? If so, how? If not, why not?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Yes. Alaska should change how it manages its fisheries, and we should start now.
 I would ban trawling within 3 miles to start. That is state water. That is our call. We are at a critical time, and we are going to have to pull some unfortunate levers. I am exhausted watching out-of-state boats and out-of-state staff come north, pull the value out of our water, and leave nothing behind. Alaskans are forced to play their game and pay the bills.
 The fish belong here. A fish in every net and every freezer on every table. Coastal towns should see the work, the product and the paycheck, not a wake and an empty plant. I will put Alaska first in every fight with federal managers and anyone else who treats our fishery like a pass-through.
 This is not about ending commercial fishing. It is about ending a system that uses Alaska and does not stay. Protect the resource. Keep the jobs. Feed our people. That is the job.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Yes. Many of the most important decisions affecting our fisheries are made by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council. For too long that Council has been controlled by Seattle-based trawl interests, and Alaskans’ voices have been sidelined. As governor, I will flip that dynamic, and nominate North Pacific Council members who will advance Alaska’s interests.
 I was one of very few legislators who took the time to testify and advocate in the North Pacific Council process, largely to support reductions in Chinook, chum, and halibut bycatch in the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea. As governor, I'd nominate members to the council to make sure our interests — not Seattle's — are represented.
 The idea is simple: Alaska fisheries should benefit Alaskans and Alaska communities.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 When Alaskans can’t put fish in their nets, fill their freezers or pass a fishing tradition down to their kids, it affects more than a balance sheet. It affects families and communities that have depended on Alaska’s fisheries for generations.
 The guiding principle should be abundance.
 When there are enough fish, commercial, sport, personal use and subsistence users can all benefit. Management should be transparent, science-based and focused on maximizing sustainable abundance. Fisheries management should be based on providing for all Alaska users of a fishery, one user should not be allowed to benefit at the expense of all other users. 
 Let’s restore the runs!
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 Subsistence
 Federal law requires that rural Alaskans be given access to hunting and fishing in Alaska, while the Alaska Constitution forbids that kind of preference. How would your administration approach subsistence hunting and fishing rights?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Rural Alaskans should be able to feed their families. That is not up for debate. How we get there is.
 Federal law created a rural preference. Our Constitution says the fish and game of Alaska are reserved to all Alaskans equally. I will not pretend those two rules are the same thing. My administration will defend the Alaska Constitution and fight to keep management in state hands. A federal system that treats Alaskans differently by ZIP code is not a long-term answer.
 The real fix is abundance and access. Grow the resource. Open hunts and fisheries that put food in freezers. Work with tribes and local advisory committees as partners, not props.
 I will not use subsistence as a wedge to import a federal takeover. I will not use the constitution as an excuse to ignore rural Alaska. Hunt. Fish. Put food on the table. Manage for all Alaskans, and make sure the people who live closest to the resource are not last in line when it matters. Abundance solves all issues.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Title VIII of ANILCA is clear: Rural and subsistence users should receive priority access to fish and wildlife. But this tension has gone unresolved for 40 years, and rural Alaskans — especially in Native communities — deserve better. My administration would start from a clear principle: Subsistence is a way of life, and protecting rural Alaskans' access to it is a priority.
 I support the rural preference and would defend it — and stop the state’s expensive litigation that seeks to undermine subsistence. We should respect settled federal law, and we should protect subsistence because it’s the right thing to do.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 For many Alaskans, hunting and fishing aren’t hobbies. They are part of how families feed themselves, teach their children and maintain traditions that go back generations.
 Dual management of fish and game is not working. Alaska should manage its fish and game, period. Alaska should protect traditional subsistence uses and local food security.
 The long-term goal should be sustainable abundance and responsible management so Alaskans can continue to use the resources this state provides.
 Let’s fill rivers and freezers again!
 Bernadette Wilson (R) 
 Candidate declined to answer questions.

 Data centers
 Alaska currently has no laws restricting or encouraging data centers. Would you favor changing that? If so, how? If not, why not?
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Yes. I favor data centers, and I favor writing the rules so Alaska wins.
 They can bring real private-sector revenue, construction jobs and long-term tax base if we do it on our terms. I will not give away the state to get a ribbon cutting. Responsible environmental management is part of the deal: siting, water, noise and land use handled upfront, not after the concrete is poured.
 Power is the test. The operators I want here produce their own generation and can put surplus back on the grid. That is how a data center helps drive down costs for all Alaskans. If a project needs to drain the Railbelt and leave families paying more, it does not belong here.
 I absolutely oppose mass surveillance and privacy infringement. Alaska should not host an industry that turns our land into a listening post. Write that into the permit. Protect Alaskans first.
 Say yes to projects that pay, power the grid and respect this state. Say no to the ones that do not.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 Yes. I am the only candidate for governor who supports a moratorium on data center construction until the legislature can pass comprehensive regulation that protects the public interest. I am especially concerned about the potential impact of data centers on the electric bills of everyday Alaskans.
 While we’re at it, I'd also support AI regulation: banning Flock cameras and similar AI-driven mass surveillance technologies, holding AI companies liable if they harm our kids, requiring disclosure of AI-generated political ads, and stronger protections for youth and seniors against AI fraud and impersonation.
 Treg Taylor (R) 
 Alaska should encourage data center development but we have to learn what has worked in the Lower 48.
 Alaska possesses unique advantages, including abundant water resources and a naturally cold climate that can significantly reduce cooling costs, one of the largest expenses for many data centers.
 At the same time, decisions should account for energy costs, local community needs, environmental stewardship and long-term economic benefits.
 My preference is to position Alaska to compete for technology investment while ensuring development is thoughtful, sustainable and beneficial to Alaskans.
 Bernadette Wilson (R)

 AI usage by state
 If elected, would you support using artificial intelligence to provide or enhance state services? Please explain.
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Yes, where it makes state government faster, cheaper and more accountable. No, where it replaces judgment or puts Alaskans’ private information at risk.
 I would use AI to cut backlog: permitting, licensing, benefit processing and the paperwork that keeps a family or a business waiting on Juneau. If a tool can flag waste, speed a road project or get a license out the door without another layer of staff, we should use it. The standard is simple. Does it improve a service Alaskans already pay for?
 I will not turn the state into an experiment. No black-box decisions on troopers, child welfare or who gets a benefit. No mass surveillance. No selling or sloppy handling of personal data. 
 Technology is a tool. The governor still answers for the result. Use it to serve Alaskans.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 
 I used to work on technology policy, which is when I first became familiar with AI. AI is a powerful tool. It has the potential to make our government much more efficient. It’s also no substitute for human judgment. I harbor deep concerns about its potential effects on our economy and society.
 Most importantly: people — not algorithms — must make the decisions that shape our lives. I would require human decision makers whenever a state agency uses AI in decisions affecting Alaskans.
 Put to good use, AI could help cut bureaucratic backlogs in permitting, Medicaid and food stamp eligibility determinations, and more. It can help our public employees do their jobs easier and faster. But AI is much more useful to Alaska in the hands of a skilled worker, or someone with institutional knowledge, than as a replacement for skilled labor and institutional knowledge.
 Alaskans' personal information belongs to Alaskans alone. It should be guarded carefully and not fed into third-party systems without consent. I support commonsense protections like a ban on Flock cameras and similar AI-driven mass surveillance technologies.

 Elections administration
 For lieutenant governor candidates: As lieutenant governor, you would be responsible for administering Alaska’s elections. Please list the changes you would make or propose to Alaska’s election laws. 
 Dave Bronson (R) 
 Rules are unclear. Deadlines are flexible. The chain of custody is inconsistent. Voter rolls are outdated. When trust breaks down, elections fail, regardless of who wins. 
 My administration would make elections visibly secure, transparent and auditable. Clear rules in law. Strong standards in practice. No excuses.
 Ballots must be received by Election Day. Election Day should mean Election Day.
 In-person voting should require a government-issued photo ID. That safeguard is used in everyday life. It should apply to elections.
 Absentee ballots should require a notarized signature. Convenience cannot come at the expense of confidence.
 Voter registration should be a deliberate act, not an automatic byproduct of unrelated programs. End automatic voter registration through the PFD. Eligible voters can always register or re-register. Registration should be intentional and verified.
 The lieutenant governor should run elections in the open. Uniform statewide standards for ballot handling, transport and documentation will protect the chain of custody. Parties and observers should have visibility at every stage.
 Recounts must be transparent, auditable and thorough. The public should see disputes resolved, not hidden behind procedure.
 Voter rolls must be cleaned regularly using death records, permanent moves and inactivity. Eligible voters must always be able to register again. Accuracy and access are not opposites.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D)

 Treg Taylor (R)

 Let’s make our elections efficient! As lieutenant governor, my focus would be on accurate voter rolls, transparent ballot processing and tabulation, clear procedures and greater public confidence in how elections are administered.  The Issues
 Dunleavy's tenure
 Gov. Mike Dunleavy is in the final year of his eight-year tenure. Name what you see as his most significant policy successes and challenges, and describe how you would have handled the policy challenges differently.
 Dave Bronson ( R )
 Gov. Dunleavy is in the last year of two terms. Credit where it is due.
 He took office after years of job losses. Unemployment is lower than in 2018. The Permanent Fund is larger. Oil production stopped sliding and started climbing. He pushed back on federal overreach, kept Alaska in the resource fight, and reopened the economy when others wanted it shut. The Alaska Reads Act showed common ground on education is possible. Those things happened on his watch.
 The kitchen table did not get the same attention. Housing is out of reach. Heat, fuel and groceries still punish working families, and rural Alaska pays the worst of it. The budget is still year to year. The gas line is still a speech. Young people are still leaving. Relationships with the Legislature broke down too often, and Alaska paid for the stalemate.
 I would have done a better job fostering relationships and working with the Legislature. A governor who cannot build a working majority does not deliver for families. Energy cost would be job one: in-state gas, generation and transmission that lower bills in Anchorage, Fairbanks and the Bush. 
 I backed Gov. Dunleavy. I respect the fights he won. The job now is the reality Alaskans live with, not the record we recite.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins ( D )
 Alaska has suffered immensely through the Dunleavy Administration. I think it’s fair to describe our governor’s eight years as a failure. Alaska has lost working-age population. Our schools are closing. Our ferry system is a shell of itself. Faith in our fisheries management is at the lowest level I can remember in my adult life. Alaskans generally feel like our state is headed in the wrong direction. Dunleavy’s vetoes, which often come without explanation, represent a failure of governance.
 My governing philosophy is the opposite: start with coalitions, not confrontation. As a legislator, I chaired the House State Affairs Committee for six years, helped build cross-partisan coalitions that passed ethics reform (banning lobbyists from buying legislators food and drink) and reduced halibut and Chinook bottom trawl bycatch at the North Pacific Council. I won five elections in a district that voted for Donald Trump by focusing on the issues that voters really care about. 
 If elected governor, I will set out goals for Alaska’s future, engage collaboratively with the legislature to move toward those goals, and finally get Alaska back on track to economic growth, stable and sustainable public services, and lower costs like electricity and housing.
 Treg Taylor ( R )
 Gov. Dunleavy deserves credit for defending Alaska’s economic future, standing up to federal overreach, advancing resource development and maintaining fiscal discipline through difficult years.
 But Alaskans are still hurting. Families are leaving. Energy costs are too high. Housing is too expensive. We’re losing population and struggling to compete. That’s not good enough for a state with Alaska’s resources and potential.
 We need to stop managing decline and start building growth. I want to open more land for Alaskans to own, accelerate infrastructure, reduce permitting delays, lower energy costs and make it easier for families to stay, work, raise their kids and build wealth here.

 The dividend should be calculated by the statutory fixed formula, not by whatever Juneau feels like that year.
 The Permanent Fund belongs to Alaskans. Unfortunately, the way it currently sits, it needs to be restored from mismanagement and overspending in Juneau (because) it can't be delivered.
 I will not support a system where legislators shrink the check to paper over spending.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins ( D )
 I think the current formula needs to be rewritten as a part of a broader fiscal compromise. In addition, I will work with the legislature to constitutionally protect the Permanent Fund from overspending so that it can grow in real terms to benefit future generations of Alaskans.

 The Permanent Fund belongs to the people of Alaska. Families count on that dividend, and they deserve a system they can actually count on from year to year.
 Alaskans are sick of the PFD becoming a political weapon. That isn’t fair to anyone. I support a sustainable constitutional framework that provides meaningful, predictable dividends while protecting the fund for future generations.
 But we also need to address the bigger problem: Alaska needs an economy strong enough that we aren’t constantly choosing between dividends and essential services. More production, more jobs, more investment and more people working in Alaska means more opportunity and less pressure on the state budget.

 School funding allocation
 Should the state change the way it allocates funding to K-12 schools? Why or why not?
 Dave Bronson ( R )
 Fund education early, and show the public where the money goes.
 Districts cannot run a school on a guess. The state should set the formula and release the funding on a calendar districts can actually plan around: how much they get, and when it hits the account. Late budgets force hiring freezes, midyear cuts and chaos for teachers and parents. That is Juneau failing the classroom.
 Districts should account for every dollar in plain language. How much reached a teacher and a classroom? How much went to administration, contracts and overhead? If the state writes the check, Alaskans have a right to see the spend. Alaska pays the second most in the country and has the worse outcomes. The problem is very apparent.
 Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins ( D )
 I support an amendment to Alaska’s Constitution to forward-fund education. Right now, districts learn how many teachers they can keep only after the annual budget fight is over, which is one of several reasons why we keep losing great educators to the Lower 48 while class sizes climb. With forward funding, school boards would know in advance what funding levels to expect from the state and have time to make well-reasoned and well-communicated decisions about their own budgets.
 Alaska should modernize the way it funds k12 education so the formula better reflects the real cost of educating students today. The current system relies on outdated assumptions and hasn’t kept pace with inflation, rising energy and insurance costs, or the unique challenges facing rural communities. That has left school districts making repeated cuts that hurt students and make it harder to recruit and retain great teachers.

 Alaskans are hurting because our education system isn’t working well enough for their kids. That’s not right.
